opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
Today's readings left me with an uncomfortable question: Where do I fit in God's plan? As a Gentile reading the Gospel of the Canaanite woman, there is tremendous hope in the story, but there is also a moment that can hurt.

The first reading from Isaiah tells us that foreigners who join themselves to the Lord, love His name, and serve Him will be welcomed. God says,  “My house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples.”  Long before Christ, God was already revealing that His plan would reach beyond Israel. Then Paul speaks about Israel and the Gentiles in Romans. The Gentiles have received mercy, but Paul makes something very clear about Israel:  “The gifts and the call of God are irrevocable.” God has not rejected His chosen people and simply replaced them with someone else. Through human disobedience, God continues working toward mercy. This doesn't mean God causes our disobedience. It means even our failures cannot defeat His plan. God can take what human beings have broken and still bring mercy from it.

Then comes the Canaanite woman. She is not one of the people of Israel, yet she comes to Jesus crying, “Have pity on me, Lord, Son of David!” Her daughter is suffering, and she believes Jesus can save her. But Jesus initially tells her, “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” He then says it is not right to take the children's food and throw it to the dogs. That is difficult to read as a Gentile. For a moment, I can almost hear, *I did not come for you. It can make me wonder whether I somehow belong less.

But this woman does something extraordinary. She doesn't walk away. She doesn't argue that Israel should lose its place so that she can have one. Instead, she answers,  “Please, Lord, for even the dogs eat the scraps that fall from the table of their masters.”  In other words: I am not asking You to take anything away from anyone else. I simply believe there is enough mercy in You for me too.  Jesus responds, “O woman, great is your faith!”  And her daughter is healed.

At first, I wondered whether Jesus was surprised by her faith. But perhaps this encounter isn't revealing something Jesus didn't know. Perhaps it is revealing something we need to know. The Canaanite woman did not change God's plan. She was already part of it. Isaiah had proclaimed that God's house would become a house of prayer for all peoples. Jesus came through Israel, fulfilling God's covenant with Israel, and through Him salvation would reach the nations. Israel's place in God's story is not erased by the inclusion of the Gentiles, and Gentiles are not inferior because salvation came through Israel. One was chosen so that eventually God's mercy could reach all.

Paul leaves no room for either group to boast. Israel needs God's mercy. Gentiles need God's mercy. The disobedient need God's mercy. The faithful live because of God's mercy. In the end, every one of us stands before God needing mercy.

That makes me look differently at the Canaanite woman. Jesus' silence did not make her leave. The disciples did not make her leave. Hearing that His mission was first to Israel did not make her leave. Even words that must have been painful did not make her leave. Why? Because somehow she already knew who He was. She called Him Lord. She believed He could save her daughter. And once she recognized Him, she wasn't going anywhere.

That may be what touches me most about this Gospel. I don't need to diminish Israel's place in God's covenant to know there is a place for me. I don't need someone else to be rejected for me to be accepted. There is enough mercy. The Canaanite woman understood that. She stood before Christ with nothing to offer except her need and her faith, trusting that even what seemed like a scrap of His mercy would be enough. And Jesus did not call her inferior. He called her faith great.

God is on my lips, and once I have come to know Him, I cannot imagine unknowing Him. Perhaps that is the faith of the Canaanite woman: I know who You are, Lord. So even when I don't completely understand where I fit, I will not walk away. I trust there is enough mercy in You for me too.
